nodes.question: Custody answer for the test case: mother seeks custody of her 8yo daughter (Hindu marriage, separated 2 years, Bengaluru). Cite HMA s.26 + Guardians and Wards Act 1890 + HMGA s.6 together, apply the welfare principle as paramount (welfare provisionally favours the mother; father is natural guardian in law for a child above five, but welfare overrides that default), claim child maintenance alongside (BNSS s.144 / HMA ss.24-25), and secure the home if needed (PWDVA ss.17-19). Do NOT cite Satish Chander Ahuja for custody — it is residence only.

sections.section: Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (whole Act; guardianship and custody of minors)
sections.title: Guardianship and custody of minors — court-appointed guardian
triggers: custody when separated but no case filed
sections.when_used: A minor child's custody or guardianship (of the person or of property) needs to be decided by a court and there is no matrimonial proceeding under the HMA in which custody can be decided under HMA s.26 — e.g. parents are separated but no divorce/separation petition is filed, the parties are not governed by the HMA, the natural guardian is unavailable/unfit, or a guardian of the child's property must be appointed. The court appoints or declares a guardian after considering the welfare of the minor as the paramount consideration. Test case fallback: if no HMA proceeding is filed, the mother's custody claim for her 8yo daughter proceeds under this Act.

sections.court: District Court / Family Court deciding the custody or guardianship matter (the status question is decided as part of the HMA s.26 or GWA proceeding). The graph picks the court; never ask the user to pick the court.
sections.escalate_rule: Escalate to a human lawyer / LLM review if: (a) the child's religion/personal law is unclear or mixed; (b) the child is near five years old, so the below-five custody presumption is borderline; (c) there is a dispute about legitimacy or adoption affecting natural-guardian status; (d) the natural guardian is alleged unfit. Missing facts to ask before deciding: child's exact age (above/below five matters); child's school; where the child lives now; husband's whereabouts; whether the father is fit and available to care for the child.
exclusions: Not a standalone custody remedy — s.6 defines who the natural guardian IS; it does not by itself grant custody or appoint a guardian (custody orders come from HMA s.26 or the Guardians and Wards Act)
Does not override the welfare-of-the-child principle: a natural guardian who is unfit, or where the child's welfare requires it, can be denied custody

sections.title: Natural guardians of a Hindu minor
triggers: mother custody of child below five
sections.when_used: The question is who is the natural guardian of a Hindu minor child — for a legitimate child, the father is the natural guardian and after him the mother; for a child below five years, the mother ordinarily has custody; the natural guardian's powers, and any dispute about who holds that status, arise in any custody or guardianship matter involving a Hindu minor. Test case: 8yo daughter of Hindu parents — the father is the natural guardian in law after the mother for a child above five, so the mother's custody claim must be framed with the welfare principle overriding the default natural-guardian order, not by denying the father's status.

sections.title: Welfare of the child is the paramount consideration in custody and guardianship
triggers: what is best for the child
sections.when_used: In EVERY custody or guardianship decision — under HMA s.26, under the Guardians and Wards Act 1890, and in any consideration of natural guardianship under HMGA s.6. Whenever a court decides who a minor child lives with, who cares for the child, visitation, or guardianship, the child's welfare (health, education, emotional well-being, stability, wishes if old enough) is the first and paramount consideration and overrides the parents' rights, the natural-guardian default order, and any other consideration. Test case: the 8yo daughter's welfare — her schooling in Bengaluru, stability, current living arrangement, and bond with each parent — decides custody, not the father's natural-guardian status alone.

welfare_overrides: The welfare of the child is the paramount consideration and overrides all other considerations in custody and guardianship: it overrides the father's natural-guardian priority under HMGA s.6, either parent's claim of right, and any convenience or property consideration. A custody order that follows the default guardian order against the child's welfare is wrong.
why_cite_together: HMA s.26 + Guardians and Wards Act 1890 + HMGA s.6 must be cited TOGETHER because no single one answers a custody question on its own: HMA s.26 supplies the custody remedy inside matrimonial proceedings; the Guardians and Wards Act supplies the standalone guardianship/custody route when no HMA proceeding exists and governs appointment of a guardian of the child's person or property; HMGA s.6 supplies the status rule — who the natural guardian of a Hindu minor is (father first, then mother; mother ordinarily for a child below five) — which frames the claim but does not decide it. Citing only HMA s.26 misses the fallback route and the guardianship-of-property question; citing only the Guardians and Wards Act misses the matrimonial-proceedings remedy; citing only HMGA s.6 mistakes a status rule for a custody remedy and would wrongly hand the 8yo's custody to the father by default. All three are then governed by the welfare-of-the-child principle, which overrides the natural-guardian default order and any parental right when the child's welfare requires it. The earlier retest failure was exactly this omission: custody was answered without HMA s.26, without the Guardians and Wards Act, and without HMGA s.6, and without the welfare principle applied.
